newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION-From the Beehive - The countdown has begun.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-From the Beehive - The countdown has begun.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Dec 10 - The countdown has begun: the governor-general is on tiptoe, the Beehive is on high alert, and the markets are ready for what they believe will be a "huge day".
New Zealand is about to get a government -- eight weeks out from the general election that those who favour the mixed member proportional system of voting hailed as a triumph for democracy.

The financial markets are saying that if the new government is a National-NZ First coalition, the Kiwi dollar might race up 50 to 80 points. And if it is a Labour-NZ First combo, the dollar might plummet 150 points.

Whichever way it goes, NZ will have a new deputy prime minister. He will be NZ First's leader Winston Peters, who will have leap-frogged a lot of his old colleagues in National to sit at the right-hand of the Prime Minister.
Whoever is the Prime Minister might have cause to worry about his proximity.
Peters, for all the thousands of words that have been written about him since NZ First was handed the power-broker baton by voters on October 12, remains an enigma.
Is he the play-boy of NZ politics, wining and dining to the small hours, or is he a politician who believes he has been marked out by destiny, as his namesake was in Britain in 1940?
There is little doubt he has milked maximum advantage out of his role in coalition negotiations.

Labour's easy assumption that NZ First would have no choice but to coalesce with it had to overcome a serious hurdle in the first weeks of negotiation. Its leaders had to learn to massage the collective ego of NZ First that it had to be taken seriously.

In concealing his own preference with such determination that no-one -- not even close associates -- can say which way NZ First is leaning 24 hours out from a decision, Peters has achieved a feat few political leaders would be able to say they could match.
Harry S. Truman once said a government is a vessel that leaks from the top. But in this instance, NZ First has proved leak-proof; and the other parties haven't had anything to leak.

Some say this is because NZ First has compartmentalised the negotiations, erecting a series of Chinese walls to prevent leakages. Others believe that not even Peters can guess which way his caucus will go as they toss up between the "reconciliation" documents drawn up with Labour and National respectively.

Potential new ministers in the NZ First-? coalition government are said to be enthusiastic to get down to work, after the hard slog of the coalition negotiations. One or two have a grasp at last of what NZ First's policy is said to be and some even want to demonstrate their enthusiasm, after they are sworn in, by swapping Ford limousines for Jeep Cherokees.

NZ First deputy leader Tau Henare is said to be keen on moving into Vogel House, currently occupied by Justice Minister Doug Graham (no room for him if Winston Peters becomes Attorney-general and Minister of Justice).
Meanwhile politicians from the Alliance are reflecting on the high cost of their leader's commitment to stay aloof from coalition negotiations.

The Alliance, which mounted the pulpit to claim it was the only party of integrity, is now saying on the one hand it would not unreasonably withhold support for the formation of a Labour-NZ First coalition, as at the same time it says it cannot be expected to sign a blank cheque of support.

The most forlorn figure in all the coalition negotiations has been Revenue Minister Peter Dunne. The sole surviving member of the United Party, which had its day in the sun as National's coalition partner during the last months of the 1993-96 term, Dunne is a living reminder to NZ First that if you don't play your cards right, you are likely to end up on the political scrap heap.
Dunne has indicated to National ministers that he is willing to be part of a coalition government, but only if he remains a minister.
You can guess what Winston Peters has said to that.
